mcqs.question: In the grid DFS for Word Search, what is the purpose of temporarily overwriting `board[r][c]` with a sentinel character like `'#'`?
options: It speeds up the character comparison at that cell
It marks the cell as part of the current path, so a later step can't walk back onto it and reuse it
It's required so the recursion can detect the base case
It permanently removes that cell from consideration for any future search
mcqs.explanation: The word-search rule is that a path can't reuse a cell, and overwriting it with a character guaranteed not to appear in the word is how the search enforces that without a separate visited structure — a later step checking that same cell sees a guaranteed mismatch. The overwrite is restored before the function returns, so it's temporary, not permanent, and it has nothing to do with detecting the base case.

mcqs.question: Compared to marking visited cells in place on the board, what does using a separate `visited` set of coordinates cost?
options: It costs correctness — a separate set produces wrong answers on some inputs
It costs extra auxiliary space proportional to the path length, on top of whatever the in-place approach would use
It costs nothing extra; both approaches use identical memory
It only costs extra time, never extra space
mcqs.explanation: A visited set needs O(word length) extra space to track path membership, while in-place marking reuses memory the board already occupies at zero extra cost — a genuine, if modest, space trade-off. Both approaches are equally correct when implemented properly, so nothing about correctness distinguishes them, and the cost is specifically extra space, not merely extra time.

mcqs.question: Why does Word Search's outer loop try every cell in the grid as a potential starting point, rather than searching for the word's first letter some other way?
options: Because DFS cannot start from an arbitrary cell — it must begin at cell (0,0)
Because the target word's first letter could occur at any position in the grid, and each occurrence is a distinct candidate start
Because trying every cell guarantees a faster average case than any alternative
It's an implementation convenience with no effect on correctness if skipped
mcqs.explanation: Any cell whose letter matches the word's first character is a legitimate place the match could begin, and there's no way to know which one (if any) leads to success without trying — so every cell is a genuine candidate, not an arbitrary choice. Skipping this step would miss valid matches entirely; it's necessary for correctness, not just a convenience, and DFS has no requirement to start at a fixed cell.

mcqs.question: You need to find all occurrences of any word from a list of 10,000 words in one large grid. Why is a shared trie a better fit than running the single-word search 10,000 times?
options: A trie eliminates the need for a base case in the recursion
A trie reduces the grid's size, making each individual search faster
A trie unifies the shared-prefix work across all words into one pass, pruning on "no matching trie child" instead of re-walking the same prefixes once per word
Running the search 10,000 times is actually faster because each individual search is simpler
mcqs.explanation: Words sharing a prefix would otherwise have that prefix's grid paths independently re-explored once per word; a trie collapses all of them into a single search where a missing trie child prunes every word sharing that prefix at once. It doesn't change the grid's actual size or remove the need for a base case, and running per-word searches is the slower approach here, not the faster one.

mcqs.question: A Word Search DFS checks `board[r][c] != word[i]` before checking that `r` and `c` are within the grid's bounds. What happens?
options: Nothing — Python automatically skips the comparison for out-of-range indices
An out-of-bounds index access raises an error the moment the search steps off an edge or corner cell
The search silently treats out-of-range cells as automatic mismatches with no error
The bug only manifests when the target word doesn't exist anywhere in the grid
mcqs.explanation: Indexing a list or array out of range raises an error immediately in most languages — there's no automatic bounds-checking skip, so the character comparison must never run before the bounds check. This surfaces on essentially any grid, not only word-absent cases, since edge and corner cells get visited during the normal course of the outer loop trying every start cell.
